reviews.text: Didn't see this recently but realized it wasnt on my Letterbox. I hate this movie. Not only do I think the acting is rough, but it feels like one big propaganda movie of "Look how brave this man is for shooting children". Dont think we should be making a guy into a hero for that

Making a heroic film about a guy that was either a racist serial killer or lied about being a racist serial killer to impress his CHUD fanbase is... certainly a choice. Either way, Chris Kyle was a morally hideous, failed human being who should never have been employed in the armed forces. This film lives in the same gutter of GWOT apologia as Zero Dark Thirty. On top of all that, though, it's just actively bad. One of the early scenes where Chris Kyle's dad pontificates at the dining room table with some weird fascist notion that violence is a gift really set the tone for the rest of this steaming three-decker coiler.

Ya know, I was expecting to completely hate this movie but it did a great job of portraying the narcissism and depravity that runs rampant in the US military. I also enjoyed the depiction of how veterans cope with their "PTSD" (it's just guilt). I don't know any PTSD patients that willingly and eagerly want to be around things that trigger their PTSD— except veterans for some reason. A dog wrestling with a child is apparently triggering but OOOOOOO they can't WAIT to get their hands back on a gun! Anyway, Rest In Piss, Chris Kyle, you absolute scum 💜

It also functions as propaganda to defend the United States' involvement in the middle east, as well as promote the military and likely increased enlistment numbers.

To be fair, American Sniper is a pretty well made film (apart from the fake baby), I found the action sequences entertaining, and Bradley Cooper’s performance was impressive given he’d mostly only been in comedies before it. The cinematography isn’t groundbreaking but there’s definitely attention to detail in the shot choices. My issues are with the screenplay. I found the strong theme of good vs evil with an unwaveringly heroic portrayal of America’s role in the Iraq war uncomfortable to watch. While bias isn’t inherently an issue, given the film is based on true events and the controversies surrounding such a significant war, I’d be concerned about someone watching the film who wasn’t aware of the context and details. His eagerness to kill (regardless of the validity of his motives) made it difficult for me to sympathise with Kyle. Furthermore, he comes across as even more unapologetically patriotic in his autobiography claiming that everyone he killed “deserved to die”. I personally find this troubling as a sentiment and wouldn’t choose to hail the person who said it to the extent Eastwood does in the film. I appreciate that since it’s based on a book, Eastwood is somewhat limited in shaping the narrative, however, I found the sequencing slightly messy and was disappointed by the dropping and ambiguity of various plot lines. I may not be the target audience for American Sniper and perhaps I’d rate it higher if I was from the US. But then I do think The Hurt Locker is an incredible film and that’s pretty American.

That meme just got real that Americans will bomb the F outta your country then make a film showing how unhappy were the soldiers after doing it lmao. As a film, this is fine. Clint Eastwood has always been a skilled director even if his politics lean conservative and Bradley Cooper really commits to the role. But the whole thing felt way too much like propaganda for me. It presents everything in such a black and white way that I genuinely couldn’t buy into it. No country walks into war as saints, especially not America and the film barely questions any of it. Maybe this hits harder for people raised inside the media bubble created by American media around the “American hero” narrative but knowing the actual history made it hard for me to fully fall for what the movie was selling.

A high-octane recruitment ad where the subtext is just a giant foam finger shouting "USA #1." Bradley Cooper cycles through his entire repertoire of three faces: 1. Squinting through a scope, 2. Squinting at his wife, and 3. Squinting at a plastic baby that clearly didn't get any of that "increased military budget" funding. It's a masterclass in the "Here is exactly why the bad guys are bad" school of subtlety, wrapped in enough Americana to make a Fourth of July parade look understated. Great if you love cinematic propaganda and very expensive sound effects; less great if you were hoping for a fourth facial expression.
